packs.title: House openings, desert records and park pages
packs.promise: Read offered house histories, collect public clues and make from actual park views.

q.s: Collect the clues that help a visitor choose where to look next.
st: Find three actual public wayfinding or shelf-area clues that a visitor can read without entering staff-only or reserved spaces. Use the current arrangement rather than expecting a particular sign or department.
For each, record the visible clue and the next public place or kind of material it helps you find. Paraphrase the sign; do not copy a book cover or page.
Follow one of those public clues a short distance at a comfortable pace. Note whether the next clue continued, refined or changed your expectation.
Make a three-item visitor record and add one sentence about how the clues work together. Keep patrons, account screens and occupied booked rooms outside it.

q.s: Collect the visible roles of a communal growing place.
st: Reach the actual opened garden through its current River Street entrance and follow the workday’s visitor directions. Stay in the learning/observation area offered to you.

Collect three currently visible garden-feature relationships, such as a planting bed meeting a path, a water-delivery feature meeting a bed or a shared learning area meeting the planted space. Do not pick crops or enter an assigned plot for a closer view.
For each, write what you saw and the role it suggests. Distinguish your interpretation from the operator’s documented communal model and Food Pantry harvest connection.

Make a three-item record and add the source-supported harvest connection in your own words. Compare one observed feature with that documented purpose, without recording a participant’s identity or claiming a harvest you did not see.

q.s: Make a small set of instructions from a real path-and-lake view.
st: Find an opened northwestern lakefront path position that leaves the walking route clear. Notice an actual path bend, a lake edge seen from the path and a nearby public-land connection.
Write a short visitor page with three original instructions: where to continue, where to pause without blocking others, and what to leave outside the visit. Base each on what you could actually see.
Add a simple three-part arrangement of your own marks for path, view and pause. Keep it a personal observation diagram rather than a traced operator map or navigation guide.
Read it once and revise a line that assumes a reserved facility, unvisited loop or view you did not find. Keep all making on your own paper or device.

packs.title: Lake paths and downtown facades
packs.promise: Connect a current gallery and pedestrian lake shore with distinct downtown exterior records.

q.s: Collect how three current works arrange their visual evidence.
st: Enter the actual opened Gallery exhibition under its current directions. Choose three works you can observe comfortably, without depending on a specific artist or format.

For each, record one arrangement between two visible elements, such as an edge meeting a field, a repeated form interrupted or a surface meeting its surrounding space. Describe relationships rather than reproducing the image or its words.
Compare two records in one sentence. Keep your observation distinct from any artist statement; do not assign a real artist a meaning the source does not state.
Write a three-item relationship record after leaving if needed. Keep your own notes as proof, leaving displayed images, poetry and interpretive text out of it.

q.t: A span and the way back
q.s: Follow one pedestrian deck in both directions.
st: Reach the opened south deck approach beside TCA and find the actual pedestrian bridge. Keep clear of bicycle circulation and use only its offered walking scope.
Walk the bounded deck to its north endpoint at a comfortable pace. Remember one relationship between an arch/cable and the deck and one change in how the south shore appears.
Turn before extending onto the north-shore trail and return along the same opened deck. Notice which bridge detail leads your attention in this direction.
Write the two observations and one outbound/return comparison after reaching the south approach. Keep your hands free while moving and make no speed or GPS claim.

q.s: Make a small invented arrival from an actual former hotel exterior.
st: Choose a permitted public exterior angle and notice one actual roof/window relationship and one way the facade meets the street. Stay outside current commercial property.

Make three small original frames on your own page: an invented traveler arrives, notices a detail and leaves. Use the two observed relationships as the setting, with simple marks rather than copied architectural plans or source-photo framing.
Add one original line to each frame. Keep the traveler’s actions explicitly imagined and avoid historical costume, a real person’s voice or a claim about a particular guest.
Add a separate factual note that the source identifies an 1899 former hotel remodeled in 1927. Do not draw a current hotel service or invented interior into the story.
